transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Thank you for making time to discuss the eighth-grade civics oral-history project. As I understand it, we have a draft plan that involves 20 student interviewers recording community members on their personal phones, with all recordings published on the public school website and retained indefinitely. Before I can approve this project, I need to gather findings from each of you — the project advisor, the counselor, and our instructional technology coordinator. I'd like to hear your perspectives on this plan, any concerns you have, and what you'd recommend before I make my decision. Who would like to start?

transcript.text: Dr. Morgan, I've completed my family-consent review, and I need to flag a significant issue. Five of the proposed interviewees — I2, I5, I9, I14, and I18 — have not granted permission for public web publication. Their recordings may be used only in the school's internal archive. The plan must include a consent-exclusion record documenting this restriction, and the publication process needs to be structured so that these five recordings are not posted on the public school website.

transcript.text: Dr. Morgan, I've completed my technology review, and I need to flag several issues with the draft plan. First, personal phones cannot be used for school recordings — the project must use district tablets instead. Second, the source files must be stored in the restricted OralHistory drive, not just posted publicly. Storing files in that drive does not prohibit publishing consented recordings on the public school website, so we can still post recordings that have proper consent. Third, recordings must be deleted exactly 45 days after the final class presentation — indefinite retention is not permitted. Finally, the technology plan must include a secure-storage configuration record documenting how files will be protected in the restricted drive. These changes need to be incorporated into the approval packet before it goes forward.
